items.title: US and Iran begin second round of nuclear talks in Geneva

featured_image.name: Iran's Araghchi arrives in Geneva for second round of nuclear talks with US

items.description:
The United States and Iran began a second round of indirect nuclear negotiations in Geneva on Tuesday, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi leading Tehran's delegation following a meeting with the head of the United Nations nuclear watchdog.[1][2][3]

The talks, mediated by Oman, come as the U.S. military bolsters its presence in the Middle East and Iran conducts live-fire exercises in the Strait of Hormuz.[4][5][6]

items.title: Scientists drill deepest-ever sediment core under Antarctic ice

featured_image.name: Record-breaking Antarctic drill reveals 23 million years of ...

items.description:
An international team of researchers has drilled a 228-meter sediment core from beneath the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, setting a record for the deepest geological sample ever retrieved from under any ice sheet. The core, which could span 23 million years of climate history, will help scientists predict how much ice may melt as the planet warms.

The achievement, announced this week by the SWAIS2C (Sensitivity of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet to 2°C) project, came on the team's third attempt after two previous Antarctic seasons were thwarted by technical challenges. The core was extracted from a location at Crary Ice Rise on the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf, more than 700 kilometers from the nearest Antarctic research stations.[1][2]

items.title: Iran begins Strait of Hormuz military drills ahead of US talks

featured_image.name: Trump sends USS Gerald R. Ford to Middle East amid Iran nuclear talks

items.description:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched extensive naval exercises in the Strait of Hormuz on February 16, demonstrating its military capabilities just one day before a critical round of nuclear negotiations with the United States in Geneva. The drills, titled "Smart Control of Hormuz Strait," were supervised by IRGC Commander Major General Mohammad Pakpour and aimed to test operational readiness against what Tehran described as "potential security and military threats," according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.[1][2][3]

The Strait of Hormuz, located between Oman and Iran, represents one of the world's most critical energy chokepoints. Approximately 20 million barrels of oil flow through the waterway daily, accounting for roughly 20% of global petroleum consumption, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. More than 80% of that crude oil is destined for Asian markets, with China, India, Japan, and South Korea as the primary recipients.[4]

items.description:
European stocks held firm on Tuesday as investors monitored the second round of nuclear negotiations between the United States and Iran in Geneva, with energy markets also showing stability despite heightened regional tensions.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 was steady in early trading, according to Reuters, as the talks between Washington and Tehran got underway. U.S. markets remained closed for the Presidents' Day holiday, limiting trading volumes across global exchanges.[1][2]

items.title: Chinese humanoid robots perform kung fu at world's most-watched TV gala

featured_image.name: Humanoid robots, kung fu masters dazzle in Spring Festival ...

items.description:
China's biggest technology firms used the Lunar New Year holiday to demonstrate the country's growing dominance in artificial intelligence and robotics, with humanoid robots performing martial arts on the world's most-watched television broadcast and several leading AI developers unveiling new flagship models.

Four robotics startups—Unitree Robotics, Galbot, Noetix, and MagicLab—displayed their humanoid machines during the 2026 Spring Festival Gala on Sunday, a China Central Television event comparable in cultural significance to the Super Bowl in the United States. The gala attracted an estimated 79% of live television viewers in China last year, according to Reuters.[1][2]

items.title: Experts say toxin that killed Navalny was lab-made, not from frogs

featured_image.name: Alexey Navalny's Very Strange Form of Freedom | The New Yorker

items.description:
The toxin that European governments say killed Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny was almost certainly manufactured in a laboratory rather than extracted from poison dart frogs in the wild, according to experts who spoke out this week following an announcement from five European nations.

Days after the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Sweden, and the Netherlands jointly declared that Navalny was poisoned with epibatidine, a neurotoxin found naturally in South American dart frogs, specialists in amphibian biology and toxicology told news outlets that obtaining the substance from live frogs would be practically impossible.[1][2]

items.title: Japan to ship carbon emissions to Malaysia in regional first

featured_image.name: Malaysia and Japan plan major cross-border carbon capture project ...

items.description:
Japan will ship carbon dioxide emissions to Malaysia in what would be the first cross-border carbon capture and storage project in Southeast Asia, a plan that is drawing criticism from climate advocates who argue the technology is more symbolic than effective in combating climate change.

Under the arrangement, emissions from Japan's polluting industries—including electric power, oil refining, cement, and steel—would be captured, liquefied, and transported by ship to depleted gas fields off the coast of Sarawak on the island of Borneo. If successful, experts say the project could pave the way for similar initiatives in other Southeast Asian nations such as Indonesia and Thailand.[1]

items.title: Kremlin rejects European findings that Russia poisoned Navalny

featured_image.name: Alexei Navalny, in his own words

items.description:
Scientists and chemical weapons experts conclude that the rare neurotoxin found in Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny's body was almost certainly synthesized in a laboratory rather than harvested from South American dart frogs, according to analysis released at the Munich Security Conference last week.

The United Kingdom, France, Germany, Sweden, and the Netherlands announced on February 14 that laboratory testing had "conclusively confirmed" the presence of epibatidine in samples taken from Navalny's body. The toxin, naturally occurring only in Ecuadorian poison dart frogs, was described as "highly likely" the cause of his death in an Arctic penal colony on February 16, 2024.[1][2][3]

items.title: EU advisers warn bloc unprepared for worsening climate change

featured_image.name: Ottmar Edenhofer reappointed to the EU Climate Advisory ...

items.description:
The European Union is unprepared for worsening climate change and must urgently increase investment to protect people and infrastructure from intensifying floods, wildfires, and severe heatwaves, independent scientific advisers warned on Monday.

The European Scientific Advisory Board on Climate Change released a report titled "Strengthening resilience to climate change – Recommendations for an effective EU adaptation policy framework," calling for a more coordinated approach across member states as the bloc faces escalating climate risks that could "undermine the EU's economic and social foundations."[1][2]
